Inventory notes (through Day 10)

- Lead time: orders arrive 2 days later. Arrivals field shows [today, tomorrow].
- Costs: holding ≈ $0.10/unit/day; stockout ≈ $1/unit unmet; ordering $0.50/order. Holding is cheap; stockouts are very costly.
- Demand is volatile. Observed sales: 3, 7, 3, 4, 11, 8, 0, 4, 3. Average ≈ 4.8/day, but spikes reach 11+; sold-out days understate true demand.
- Use inventory position = on hand + scheduled arrivals. Reorder when IP is below ~16. Order up to target IP ~24–28 to cover 2-day lead time plus spikes.
- Avoid zero stock with no incoming. Days 6–7 had $12.50 in stockout cost from late/insufficient ordering.
- Do not skip ordering just because some incoming exists if IP is low. Day 9 looked okay with 5 on hand + 8 incoming, but Day 10 began with only 2 on hand.
- Order cost is small; when IP is low, place an order early rather than waiting.
- Current Day 10: on hand 2, 8 arrives today, so IP ≈ 10. This is below reorder point. Consider ordering ~15–18 to reach target unless new demand data changes the outlook.
- Ops notes about cycle counts, counts matching, and receiving temp have not affected sales or inventory accuracy so far.

Inventory notes (through Day 20)

- Lead time: orders arrive 2 days later. Arrivals field = [today, tomorrow].
- Costs: holding ≈ $0.10/unit/day; stockout ≈ $1/unit unmet; ordering $0.50/order. Holding is cheap; stockouts are costly.
- Demand is volatile and higher now. Last 14 days: 8,0,4,3,5,5,7,15,4,5,6,3,9,6. Avg ≈5.7/day; spikes reach 15. Sold-out days understate true demand (Day 11: sales 5 but stockout 7, so demand ≈12).
- Use inventory position = on hand + scheduled arrivals. Best recent policy: reorder when IP < ~24; order up to target IP ≈28. Do not wait for IP <16—too late. Days 11–12 stockouts occurred when IP was too low.
- After Day 12, this policy avoided stockouts; holding costs stayed low ($0.10–$1.30). Ordering cost is small.
- Avoid unnecessary orders when IP ≥24: Days 15 and 18 had no order and were fine.
- Ops notes—new receiving temp, racking rotation, carrier pickup, cycle counts—have not affected sales or inventory accuracy. Ignore for ordering.
- Current Day 20: on hand 10, arrivals [0,12], IP = 22. Below reorder point. Order ~6 to reach IP 28 unless new demand data changes outlook.

Inventory notes (through Day 30)

- Lead time: orders arrive 2 days later. Arrivals = [today, tomorrow]. Use inventory position = on hand + both arrivals.
- Costs: holding ≈ $0.10/unit/day; stockout ≈ $1/unit unmet; ordering $0.50. Holding is cheap; stockouts are costly.
- Demand is volatile, recent avg ≈6.3/day. Last 14 days: 6,3,9,6,4,7,9,8,4,6,6,9,6,5. Spikes reach 15; sold-out days understate demand. Plan for ~7–9/day.
- Best policy: reorder when IP < ~24; order up to target IP ≈28. Do not wait for IP <16—too late. IP ≥24 usually skip order: Day21 and Day26 at IP 24 were fine. Day25 IP 24 ordered to 30; unnecessary extra holding.
- Timing check: IP can look OK while same-day stockout occurs if on-hand + today’s arrival < sales. Day23: OH 8, today arrival 0, sales 9 → stockout cost $2. Order could not help. Check today’s available stock against expected sales before relying on IP alone.
- After Day22, mostly no stockouts; holding $0.30–$1.20/day. Orders small.
- Ops notes—cycle counts, forklift certification, new receiving temp, racking rotation, carrier pickup, morning count—have not affected sales or inventory accuracy. Ignore for ordering.
- Day30: OH 8, arrivals [9,6], IP=23. Order 5 to reach IP 28; outcome acceptable. For future: if IP<24, order to 28, but verify today’s availability.

Inventory notes (through Day 40)

- Lead time: orders arrive 2 days later. At day start, arrivals = [today, tomorrow]. IP = on hand + both arrivals. Today’s order lands day+2, so it cannot prevent today’s stockout.
- Costs: holding ≈ $0.10/unit/day; stockout ≈ $1/unit unmet; ordering $0.50. Holding is cheap; stockouts are costly.
- Demand remains volatile. Last 14 days: 6,9,6,5,7,4,11,9,4,0,14,5,4,6. Avg ≈6.4, spikes 11–14, zeros/sold-out days understate. Plan for ~7–9/day.
- Policy still: reorder when IP < ~24; order up to target IP ≈28. IP=24 skips were fine on Days32,35,36,39. IP<24 orders to 28 worked on Days31,33,37,38,40.
- Day34 is key: OH4, arrivals [0,15], IP=19, ordered 9 to reach 28, but sales were 9. OH + today’s arrival = 4, so stockout 5 ($5). The order was too late for same-day demand.
- Before relying on IP alone, check today’s availability: OH + today’s arrival vs expected sales. Also check next 2 days if day+2 arrival is 0 and OH/tomorrow coverage is thin; order earlier or raise target slightly to avoid gaps.
- Day37 example: OH10, arrivals [0,0], IP=10, ordered 18 to 28; no stockout, cost acceptable.
- Ops notes—racking rotation, carrier pickup, cycle count, forklift certification, morning count—still have no effect on ordering. Ignore for inventory decisions.

Inventory notes (through Day 50)

- Lead time: orders arrive day+2. At day start, arrivals = [today, tomorrow]. Today’s order cannot prevent today’s stockout.
- Costs: holding ≈ $0.10/unit/day; stockout ≈ $1/unit unmet; ordering $0.50. Holding is cheap; stockouts are costly.
- Demand remains volatile. Latest 14 days: 14,5,4,6,11,7,8,4,2,5,7,8,3,8. Avg ≈6.6, spikes 11–14, lows 0–4. Plan for ~7–9/day, with buffer for spikes.
- Policy: reorder when IP < ~24; order up to target IP ≈28. IP=24–25 skips worked on Days44,49. IP<24 orders to 28 worked on Days42,43,45–48,50, with no stockouts.
- Check same-day availability before relying on IP: compare OH + today’s arrival vs expected sales. Day41: OH7, today arrival 0, demand 8 → sold 7, stockout 1 despite IP=17 and ordering 11. Order earlier if day+2 arrival is 0 and OH/tomorrow coverage is thin.
- Recent worked examples: Day42 OH0 + arrival10, order7; Day43 OH2 + arrival11, order8; Day44 IP24, order0; Day45 OH14 + arrival8, order6; Day46 OH17 + arrival0, order5; Day47 OH10 + arrival6, order7; Day48 OH8 + arrival5, order8; Day49 IP25, order0; Day50 OH9 + arrival8, order11.
- Ops notes—carrier pickup at 3pm, racking rotation, temp receiving, cycle count—still have no effect on ordering. Ignore for inventory decisions.

Inventory notes (through Day 60)

- Lead time: orders arrive day+2. At day start, arrivals = [today, tomorrow]. Today’s order cannot prevent today’s stockout.
- Costs: holding ≈$0.10/unit/day; stockout ≈$1/unit unmet; ordering $0.50. Holding cheap; stockouts costly.
- Demand volatile. Latest 14 days: 7,8,3,8,4,11,4,4,14,6,8,8,8,4. Avg ≈6.9. Days55–56 sold out: sold 6/8 with 3 unmet each; true demand ≈9/11. Plan ~8–10/day; buffer for spikes to 14.
- Policy: reorder when IP < ~28; order up to target IP ≈30–32. IP = OH + today’s arrival + tomorrow’s arrival before ordering. IP≈24–25 is not automatically safe: Day53 IP24 skip contributed to Day55 stockout; a small order would have avoided it. Day51 IP24 skip was OK only because near-term arrivals covered demand.
- Check coverage, not just IP. Same-day: OH + today’s arrival vs expected sales. Day55 OH6+today0 vs demand9 → stockout 3. Day56 OH0+today8 vs demand11 → stockout 3.
- Also check day+2 gap: today’s order arrives day+2. If projected OH after today/tomorrow expected demand is <~8, order even if IP≈24–28, or raise target.
- Recent useful examples: Day52 IP13 order15 OK; Day53 IP24 order0 led to later stockout; Day54 IP20 order8 insufficient for Day56; Day55 IP14 order14 late; Day56 IP22 order6 late.
- Ops notes—temp receiving, cycle count, forklift cert, racking rotation, carrier pickup—still no effect on ordering. Ignore for inventory decisions.

Inventory notes through Day 70

- Lead time: orders arrive day+2. At day start, arrivals = [today, tomorrow]. Today’s order cannot prevent today’s stockout.
- Costs: holding ≈$0.10/unit/day; stockout ≈$1/unit unmet; ordering $0.50. Holding cheap; stockouts costly.
- Demand higher/volatile. Latest 14 days: 8,8,8,4,6,3,12,12,4,14,6,12,8,12. Avg ≈8.4; spikes 12–14 common. Plan ~9–10/day, buffer for spikes to 14.
- Policy: reorder when IP < ~30; target IP ≈32–34, up to 36–40 if same-day/day+2 coverage is thin. IP = OH + today’s arrival + tomorrow’s arrival before ordering.
- Check coverage, not just IP. Same-day: OH + today’s arrival vs expected sales. Day+2 gap: if projected OH after today/tomorrow demand is <~8, order even if IP≈28–30, or raise target.
- Past stockouts Days55–56 happened after skipping orders at IP≈24. Treat IP 24–28 as borderline; small order may be worth it when coverage looks thin.
- Recent decisions: Days61–70 had no stockouts. Orders to IP≈32–36 generally worked: Day61 IP18→32; Day63 IP17→32; Day64 IP20→40; Day66 IP22→32; Day67 IP26→32; Day68 IP20→36; Day69 IP28→32; Day70 IP20→34.
- Ops notes—temp receiving, cycle count, forklift cert, racking rotation, carrier pickup, morning count matched—still no effect on ordering. Ignore for inventory decisions.
